name: Pairwise Comparison and Statistical Significance
question: Is version B really better, or is it noise?
summary: When two versions of a prompt, model or agent are compared, the question is not “what score did B get” but “how often is B better than A on the same inputs, and could that be chance”. Pairwise comparison shows a judge (human or LLM) both answers to each question and asks which is better, in both orders to cancel position bias. The result is a win rate with a confidence interval; if the interval includes 50%, the data cannot tell the versions apart. Sample size sets the interval width, so it is chosen before running. Many versions can be ranked with a Bradley–Terry or Elo model fitted to pairwise results. Writing good rubrics and calibrating judges is covered by LLM-as-a-Judge; this technique is about comparing and deciding.
useCases: Deciding whether to ship a new prompt, model or retrieval change
Ranking several candidate models on your own tasks
Reporting eval results with error bars instead of single numbers

judges often favour the first or second slot; run both orders and count split verdicts as ties
about ±1.96 × √(p(1−p)/n); about ±3.5 points at n=800 and ±7 at n=200
ship only if the lower bound is above 50%, or a paired test gives p below your threshold
decide in advance from the smallest gain worth detecting
turn many pairwise results into a ranking with uncertainty

comparison.scope: Two versions on the same inputs

code.text: second = judge(q, b, a)           # same pair, swapped
if first == "2" and second == "1": return 1.0      # B wins both
if first == "1" and second == "2": return 0.0      # A wins both
scores = [verdict(q, a, b) for q, a, b in zip(qs, A, B)]
wins = sum(s == 1.0 for s in scores); losses = sum(s == 0.0 for s in scores)

steps.title: Fix the question set first
steps.text: Kaveri Bank, a fictional bank, samples 800 real loan queries before looking at any results, so it cannot pick questions that flatter the new prompt.

steps.title: Answer the same questions
steps.text: Both versions answer every question. Paired answers remove the difference in difficulty between questions.

steps.title: Judge in both orders
steps.text: Its judge prefers the first slot by about 10 points. Each pair is judged as A,B and as B,A; if the verdicts disagree, the pair is a tie.

steps.title: Compute the win rate
steps.text: B wins 56% of pairs, ties counted as half.

steps.title: Add the interval
steps.text: ±1.96 × √(0.56 × 0.44 ÷ 800) ≈ ±3.4 points, so 53% to 59%. The whole interval is above 50%: ship.

steps.title: Check with a paired test
steps.text: A sign test on decisive pairs gives the same answer. With only 200 questions, the interval would be 49% to 63% and the right call would be “not proven”.

Pairing on the same questions removes difficulty noise

practice.scenario: Kaveri Bank, a fictional bank, has a new prompt for its loan-query assistant. On 50 questions it looked better, but the interval ran from 42% to 70%. It fixes 800 real queries in advance, answers each with both versions, and has an LLM judge compare every pair in both orders, because the judge favours the first slot. B wins 56% of pairs with a 95% interval of 53% to 59%, entirely above 50%, so the bank ships it. Judging cost ₹960.

library.name: SciPy
library.what: binomtest gives an exact sign test and a confidence interval for the win rate.

practice.note: Store verdicts from both orders so you can measure how often the judge disagrees with itself; a high split rate means the rubric or the judge needs work.

samples.code:
import json
from scipy.stats import binomtest

rows = [json.loads(l) for l in open("verdicts.jsonl")]   # {"ab": "2", "ba": "1"} per pair
wins = sum(r["ab"] == "2" and r["ba"] == "1" for r in rows)
losses = sum(r["ab"] == "1" and r["ba"] == "2" for r in rows)
ties = len(rows) - wins - losses

win_rate = (wins + 0.5 * ties) / len(rows)
test = binomtest(wins, wins + losses, 0.5)
ci = test.proportion_ci(confidence_level=0.95)
print(f"win rate {win_rate:.1%}; ties {ties}; decisive-pair CI {ci.low:.1%}-{ci.high:.1%}; p={test.pvalue:.4f}")

interview.question: How do you decide whether a new prompt is better?
interview.answer: Run both on the same fixed question set, judge each pair in both orders, compute B’s win rate with a 95% interval, and ship only if the interval is above 50%. Choose the sample size beforehand from the smallest gain worth detecting.

interview.question: Why judge both orders?
interview.answer: LLM judges have position bias. Swapping the order and treating split verdicts as ties cancels the bias; the split rate also shows how consistent the judge is.
